title: High RAM (memory) usage
causes: Too many open programs or browser tabs, a program with a memory leak, too many startup programs, malware, or simply too little installed RAM for the workload.
steps: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), go to the Processes tab and click the Memory column to sort by usage. Note which programs use the most.
Save your work and close programs or browser tabs you do not need.
If one program keeps growing in memory over time, restart that program (this is a typical sign of a memory leak) and check for an update for it.
Restart the computer to clear memory held by long-running processes.
Open Task Manager > Startup apps and disable unneeded programs that start with Windows.
Run a scan with Windows Security (Virus & threat protection).
If RAM stays above about 85-90% even with few programs open, the PC probably needs more RAM; ask IT support about an upgrade.
warnings: Do not end processes you do not recognise; ending a Windows system process can make the system unstable.
Save your work before closing programs.

title: Slow Windows startup / slow boot
causes: Too many programs launching at startup, an old hard disk drive (HDD), a nearly full disk, pending updates, or background scans right after boot.
steps: Open Task Manager > Startup apps and look at the 'Startup impact' column. Disable high-impact programs you do not need at startup.
Check free disk space (Settings > System > Storage). A nearly full system drive slows Windows down.
Install pending Windows updates (Settings > Windows Update) and restart.
Wait a few minutes after logging in; Windows Update and antivirus scans can temporarily use a lot of resources.
Run a Windows Security scan to rule out malware.
If the PC still uses a traditional hard disk drive, an SSD upgrade is the most effective hardware fix; ask IT support.
warnings: Disabling a startup entry does not uninstall the program, but do not disable security software or drivers you do not recognise.

title: Low disk space
causes: Large downloads, video or photo files, temporary files, old Windows update files, or many installed programs.
steps: Open Settings > System > Storage to see what uses the most space.
Turn on Storage Sense, or use 'Temporary files' in the Storage page to remove temporary files and empty the Recycle Bin.
Review the Downloads folder and delete files you no longer need.
Uninstall programs you no longer use (Settings > Apps > Installed apps).
Move large personal files (videos, photos) to an external drive or cloud storage.
Aim to keep at least 10-15% of the drive free.
warnings: Never delete files from the Windows or System32 folders to free space.
Do not use 'registry cleaner' tools.
Back up important files before deleting anything you are unsure about.

title: Wi-Fi connection problems
causes: Wi-Fi turned off or airplane mode on, router problems, weak signal, wrong saved password, or an outdated or faulty wireless driver.
steps: Check that Airplane mode is off and Wi-Fi is switched on (Settings > Network & internet).
Check whether other devices can connect to the same network. If none can, the router or ISP is the likely cause.
Restart the router: unplug it for 30 seconds, plug it back in and wait a few minutes.
Click the Wi-Fi network > 'Forget', then reconnect and re-enter the password.
Move closer to the router to test whether signal strength is the problem.
Run the troubleshooter: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Network and Internet.
Install pending Windows updates, which may include a newer wireless driver.
warnings: 'Network reset' removes all saved Wi-Fi networks and VPN settings; use it only as a last resort and make sure you know your Wi-Fi password.
Do not change router admin settings if you are not sure what they do.

title: DNS resolution failures (websites not found)
keywords: websites not loading but internet works
causes: The DNS server from the ISP or router is not responding, a corrupted DNS cache, a VPN or proxy interfering, or incorrect DNS settings on the computer.
steps: Test whether the problem affects all websites and all browsers, and whether another device on the same network has the same problem.
Restart the router and the computer.
Turn off any VPN or proxy and test again.
In Command Prompt you can run 'ipconfig /flushdns' yourself; it only clears the local DNS cache and is safe.
Try automatic DNS first (Settings > Network & internet > your connection > DNS server assignment). If that does not help, a public DNS such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 can be tested.
warnings: Write down your current DNS settings before changing them so you can restore them.
On a company or university network, do not change DNS settings without permission from IT support.

title: No internet connection
causes: ISP outage, a router or modem fault, a loose cable, a disabled network adapter, or misconfigured VPN or proxy settings.
steps: Check whether other devices (phone, other PC) have internet. If none do, the problem is the router, modem or ISP, not your computer.
Check cables and router lights. Make sure the Ethernet cable is firmly connected, or Wi-Fi is on.
Restart modem and router: unplug for 30 seconds, plug back in, wait about 3 minutes.
Restart the computer.
Turn off any VPN or proxy and test again.
Run the troubleshooter: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Network and Internet.
If everything else works but only certain websites fail, see the DNS entry. If the router shows no connection, contact the ISP.
warnings: Do not reset the router to factory settings unless you have the ISP login details; you may lose the connection configuration.

title: Printer not responding or not printing
causes: Printer powered off or offline, cable or network connection problem, stuck jobs in the print queue, wrong default printer, or an outdated or missing driver.
steps: Check that the printer is on, has paper and ink or toner, and shows no error light or message. Clear any paper jam following the printer manual.
Check the connection: USB cable firmly plugged in, or printer on the same network for Wi-Fi printers.
Open Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners, select the printer and open the print queue. Cancel stuck jobs.
Make sure the correct printer is selected as default and is not set to 'Use printer offline'.
Restart the printer and the computer.
If it still fails, remove the printer and add it again, or install the latest driver from the printer manufacturer's official website.
warnings: Switch the printer off and unplug it before opening it to clear a paper jam.
Download drivers only from the manufacturer's official website.

title: Windows application crashes or freezes
causes: A bug in the application, an outdated version, corrupted program files, missing Windows updates, low RAM or disk space, or a conflict with other software.
steps: Restart the application and the computer.
Check whether the application has an update and install it.
Install pending Windows updates.
Check free RAM and disk space; crashes are more common when either is almost full.
For apps installed from Microsoft Store or listed in Settings > Apps > Installed apps, open Advanced options and try 'Repair' first.
Open Reliability Monitor (search 'View reliability history') to see when and how often the application failed, and note any error text.
If the problem remains, uninstall and reinstall the application from its official source.
warnings: 'Reset' in the app's Advanced options can delete the app's local data; back up first and try 'Repair' before 'Reset'.
Only download installers from the official vendor website.

title: High CPU usage
causes: A busy or misbehaving program, background tasks such as Windows Update, indexing or antivirus scans, too many browser tabs or extensions, malware, or an overheating CPU that is throttling.
steps: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), Processes tab, and click the CPU column to see which program uses the most.
If it is a normal program, save your work, close it and reopen it.
If it is Windows Update, search indexing or Windows Security, wait 10-20 minutes; these tasks are often temporary.
Close unneeded browser tabs and disable browser extensions you do not use.
Restart the computer, then check Task Manager again.
Run a Windows Security scan to rule out malware.
If the fan is very loud or the laptop is very hot, make sure the vents are not blocked and the laptop stands on a hard surface.
warnings: Do not end processes you do not recognise; some are essential Windows processes.
Do not install 'CPU booster' or 'PC cleaner' programs.

title: Windows Update problems
causes: Not enough free disk space, an interrupted download, corrupted update files, a pending restart, an unstable internet connection, or software conflicts.
steps: Make sure the PC has a stable internet connection and plenty of free disk space (at least 10-20 GB for major updates).
Restart the computer, then open Settings > Windows Update and click 'Check for updates' again.
Run the troubleshooter: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update.
Disconnect non-essential USB devices and external drives, then retry.
Check that the date, time and time zone are correct.
Note the exact error code; it can be searched on Microsoft's support website or given to IT support.
warnings: Do not turn off the computer while an update says 'Working on updates'; it can take a long time.
Download updates only through Windows Update or Microsoft's official website.
Back up important files before a major Windows update.

title: Slow internet speed
causes: Weak Wi-Fi signal, network congestion, large background downloads or cloud sync, a VPN, router problems, or a problem on the ISP side.
steps: Run a speed test (for example in your browser) and compare it with the speed in your ISP plan. If possible, test with an Ethernet cable as well.
Check whether other devices are also slow.
Move closer to the router, or use the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band if your router offers it.
Pause large downloads, game updates and cloud sync (OneDrive, Google Drive) and close streaming apps.
Turn off VPN temporarily and test again.
Restart the router. If the speed is still much below your plan, contact the ISP.
warnings: Do not install 'internet booster' programs; they do not work and may be malware.

title: Blue screen (BSOD) or unexpected restarts
causes: A faulty or incompatible driver, recently installed software or updates, failing RAM or disk, overheating, or corrupted system files.
steps: Write down or photograph the stop code shown on the blue screen (for example 'CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED').
Think about what changed recently (new driver, update, software, hardware) and note it.
Install pending Windows updates, which often contain driver fixes.
Free up disk space and check that the PC is not overheating.
To test RAM, search for 'Windows Memory Diagnostic' and run it (it restarts the computer).
If the PC cannot start normally, it may be possible to use Safe Mode, but this is a good point to contact IT support.
warnings: If blue screens are frequent, back up your important files as soon as possible.
Avoid 'driver updater' and 'registry cleaner' tools; they often cause more problems.
Do not try to reinstall Windows without a backup of your data.
